books.section: The Rise of the Service Sector
Prosperity and a New World Order (1988–2000)

stem: Which of the following best describes the change shown in the chart?

options.text: Manufacturing jobs grew steadily as a share of all American jobs
options.misconception: The line falls at every step, from 25 percent to 9 percent; it never grows.

options.text: Manufacturing output collapsed even as factory jobs held steady
options.misconception: The chart measures jobs, not output. Background: American factory output kept growing as machines did more of the work.

options.text: Manufacturing jobs shrank steadily as a share of all American jobs
Service jobs disappeared while factory jobs stayed flat
options.misconception: Background: service jobs grew while factory jobs shrank; the falling line is the factory side of that shift.

rationales.A: The line falls at every step, from 25 percent to 9 percent, so the share shrank rather than grew.
rationales.B: Background: the chart measures jobs, not output, and American factory output kept growing as machines did more of the work.
rationales.C: The chart shows manufacturing's share falling at every step, from 25 percent in 1970 to 9 percent in 2010.
rationales.D: Background: service jobs grew while factory jobs shrank; the falling line is the factory side of that shift.
rationales.general:
1. Read the line like a story: it starts at 25 percent in 1970 and ends at 9 percent in 2010.
2. Ask what a falling share means: factories held a smaller slice of the jobs pie at every step.
3. Keep jobs and output apart. Background: the chart counts jobs, and factory output kept growing.
4. The shift ran one way for forty years, with no step back up.
Remember: a shrinking slice is not a vanished pie — factories made more with fewer workers.

stimulus.source_note: Chart plotted from U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics, Table B-1 (annual averages); shares computed from published employment levels.
stimulus.text:
| Year | Manufacturing share of all U.S. jobs |
| 1970 | 25% |
| 1980 | 21% |
| 1990 | 16% |
| 2000 | 13% |
| 2010 | 9% |

Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics, Table B-1 (annual averages); shares computed from published employment levels.
